title: Thyroid Eye Disease & Proptosis: The Definitive Clinical Roadmap
summary: A comprehensive guide to Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), covering detailed clinical manifestations, Rundle's Curve, EUGOGO classification, and advanced management of sight-threatening complications like optic neuropathy and exposure keratopathy.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: Multi-Scenario Analysis
sections.content:
Scenario 1: Asymmetrical proptosis (RT/LT), RT severe upper eyelid retraction, LT mild upper and lower eyelid retraction. RT lid lag on down gaze (von Graeve sign).
Scenario 2: Bilateral scleral show with lid retraction and temporal flare, bilateral proptosis, bilateral conjunctival hyperemia with injection in caruncle and plica, bilateral eyelid swelling and hyperemia. Cornea appears clear; pupils are round and regular. Clinical assessment must include spontaneous and gaze-evoked orbital pain.
Scenario 3: Bilateral periorbital puffiness, lid retraction, bilateral proptosis (more prominent on RT), bilateral conjunctival hyperaemia (flare of recti).
Scenario 4: Bilateral eyelid retraction with mild edema, bilateral globe plugging, bilateral conjunctival congestion, staring appearance (Kocher sign). Central corneal reflex present, no anisocoria.

sections.title: EUGOGO Severity Classification
content: 1. Sight Threatening: Due to optic neuropathy or exposure keratopathy with corneal breakdown.
2. Moderate–Severe: One or more of: moderate-severe soft tissue involvement, lid retraction ≥ 2 mm, diplopia, proptosis ≥ 3 mm.
3. Mild: Only a minor impact on daily life.

sections.title: Clinical Activity Score (CAS)
content: Assign 1 point for each feature. Treatment considered for score ≥ 3/7:
1. Spontaneous orbital pain.
2. Gaze-evoked orbital pain.
3. Eyelid swelling (active/inflammatory phase).
4. Eyelid erythema.
5. Conjunctival redness (active/inflammatory phase).
6. Chemosis.
7. Inflammation of caruncle or plica.

content.explanation: 1. Soft tissue involvement. 2. Lid retraction. 3. Proptosis. 4. Optic neuropathy. 5. Restrictive myopathy.

sections.title: Major Risk & Poor Prognostic Factors
content: Smoking: The major clinical risk factor.
Gender: Women are 5x more likely to be affected.
Treatment: Radioactive iodine treatment of TED can exacerbate condition.

sections.title: Clinical Assessment of Proptosis
content: Step 1: Visual Inspection - Observe from above (eyebrows to chin) to detect mild differences/globe displacement.
Step 2: Measurement - Ideally use Hertel exophthalmometer; if unavailable, use a ruler on the lateral bony orbital margin.
Step 3: History - Note duration, onset, progression, pain, vision changes (BOV), and diplopia.
Step 4: Palpation & Dynamics - Assess retropulsion, thrills/pulsation (CCF), and Valsalva maneuvers (varix/haemangioma).
Step 5: Complication Check - Evaluate optic nerve function (VA, RAPD, Ishihara), EOM restrictions, and corneal health (exposure).

sections.title: How to Perform Hertel Exophthalmometry
sections.content: Ask for permission. The Hertel ophthalmometer measures the globe position from the lateral orbital rim to the corneal apex. The device uses 45-degree mirrors to visualize the scale and corneal apex simultaneously. Place notches on the lateral orbital rim using the smallest base possible. While the patient fixates straight ahead, measure the apex using the millimeter scale.

sections.title: Rundle's Curve: Natural History
sections.content: TED follows a predictable course: 1. Active Phase (increasing severity). 2. Regression Phase (declining severity). 3. Inactive Plateau Phase. These time courses vary per patient (Rundle a to d) and categorize disease as mild, moderate, marked, or severe.

sections.title: Management of Optic Neuropathy
content: 1. Primary Medical: Pulsed IV methylprednisolone (0.5–1 g for 3 successive days) then oral prednisolone (e.g., 40 mg/day).
2. Alternate Medical: 0.5–1 g IV methylprednisolone on alternate days (3–6 times, cumulative dose < 8g to prevent liver compromise).
3. Biological Therapy: Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor) to reduce proptosis and CAS score.
4. Radiation: Orbital radiotherapy combined with steroids.
5. Surgical: Orbital wall and/or orbital apex decompression if steroids are ineffective or contraindicated.

sections.title: Supportive & General Management
content: Multidisciplinary input (Endocrinologist/Orthoptist).
Meticulous control of thyroid function.
Smoking cessation (Critical).
Symptomatic: Lubricants, tinted glasses, bed-head elevation, prisms for diplopia.
Gastric protection: PPIs and osteoporosis prophylaxis for steroid users.
Exposure Keratopathy care: BCL, night tapping, moist chamber goggles, punctal plugs.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Red Flags
content: Always check Optic Nerve Function: VA, RAPD, Ishihara, and check for choroidal folds.
Liver Safety: Maintain cumulative IV methylprednisolone dose below 8g.
Differential Check: If proptosis is pulsating, consider CCF or sphenoid wing dysplasia; if Valsalva-positive, consider varix.
Baseline Requirement: Ensure gastric protection (PPI) when starting high-dose steroids.
